title: IOCL Quality Control Chemist - Mock Test 3
instructions: Test contains conceptual and instrumental analysis problems for High Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) based on detailed instrumentation flow.
Each question carries 1 mark. Read the explanations and detailed SVG schematics carefully after submitting.

questions.question: An HPLC system is being set up in an analytical lab using a mixture of methanol and water in the solvent reservoirs. If the degasser unit is bypassed and dissolved helium gas remains in the mobile phase, what will be the direct negative impact on the detector baseline?

options.A: The baseline will become completely flat, but retention time will double.
options.B: Spurious peaks and high baseline noise/drift will be created due to micro-bubbles passing through the detector flow cell.
options.C: The column length will increase from 2-10 cm to 25 cm.
options.D: The pump pressure will drop from 6000 psi to zero.

questions.explanation: Dissolved gases (like oxygen or air) when passing through the detector cell under a pressure drop form bubbles that produce erratic spikes, high noise, and baseline drift. Therefore, sonication or sparging with helium/degassers are used[span_0](start_span)[span_0](end_span).

questions.question: In HPLC instrumentation, the pump's role is to push solvent at high pressure (up to 6000 psi) at a normal flow rate (e.g., 1.2 ml/min). If gradient elution needs to be run, what is the role of the mixing valve?
questions.diagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 180' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='180' fill='#f8fafc' rx='8'/><text x='300' y='22' font-size='13' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1e293b' font-family='sans-serif'>Solvent Reservoirs & Mixing Valve Unit</text><rect x='40' y='40' width='35' height='55' rx='4' fill='#cbd5e1' stroke='#334155' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='57' y='72' font-size='9' text-anchor='middle' fill='#0f172a' font-family='sans-serif'>Solv A</text><rect x='85' y='40' width='35' height='55' rx='4' fill='#cbd5e1' stroke='#334155' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='102' y='72' font-size='9' text-anchor='middle' fill='#0f172a' font-family='sans-serif'>Solv B</text><line x1='57' y1='95' x2='57' y2='120' stroke='#0284c7' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='102' y1='95' x2='102' y2='120' stroke='#0284c7' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='57' y1='120' x2='160' y2='120' stroke='#0284c7' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='102' y1='120' x2='160' y2='120' stroke='#0284c7' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='180' cy='120' r='18' fill='#fde047' stroke='#a16207' stroke-width='2'/><text x='180' y='124' font-size='10' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#713f12' font-family='sans-serif'>Mix</text><line x1='198' y1='120' x2='260' y2='120' stroke='#0284c7' stroke-width='2.5'/><rect x='260' y='100' width='60' height='40' rx='4' fill='#93c5fd' stroke='#1d4ed8' stroke-width='2'/><text x='290' y='124' font-size='11' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1e3a8a' font-family='sans-serif'>Pump</text><line x1='320' y1='120' x2='380' y2='120' stroke='#0284c7' stroke-width='2.5'/><text x='450' y='124' font-size='11' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#0f172a' font-family='sans-serif'>To Column (Gradient Elution)</text></svg>

options.A: It manually loads the sample into the loop injector.
options.B: It mixes liquids from multiple solvent reservoirs by changing their ratio over time.
options.C: It protects the column from stripping problems.
options.D: It measures the bulk property of the detector.

questions.explanation: The mixing valve is connected before or along with the pump to blend compositions from different solvent reservoirs (such as organic solvent and water) for gradient elution[span_1](start_span)[span_1](end_span).

questions.question: A guard column (pre-column) typically has a length of 2-10 cm. What is its primary purpose?
questions.diagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 500 160' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='500' height='160' fill='#f8fafc' rx='8'/><text x='250' y='25' font-size='13' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1e293b' font-family='sans-serif'>Guard Column Protection Mechanism</text><line x1='50' y1='90' x2='120' y2='90' stroke='#0284c7' stroke-width='3'/><rect x='120' y='70' width='70' height='40' rx='4' fill='#86efac' stroke='#166534' stroke-width='2'/><text x='155' y='95' font-size='11' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#14532d' font-family='sans-serif'>Guard Col</text><text x='155' y='125' font-size='9' text-anchor='middle' fill='#dc2626' font-family='sans-serif'>Traps Impurities</text><line x1='190' y1='90' x2='260' y2='90' stroke='#0284c7' stroke-width='3'/><rect x='260' y='55' width='120' height='70' rx='6' fill='#fca5a5' stroke='#991b1b' stroke-width='2'/><text x='320' y='95' font-size='12' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#7f1d1d' font-family='sans-serif'>Analytical Column</text></svg>

options.A: To protect the analytical column life by trapping strongly bound impurities and particulate matter.
options.B: To compress the solvent up to 6000 psi.
options.C: To measure refractive index and conductivity simultaneously.
options.D: To control the flow splitting valve.

questions.explanation: The guard column is placed before the main analytical column so that debris, impurities, or irreversible contaminants are caught beforehand, preventing damage to the main column[span_2](start_span)[span_2](end_span).

questions.question: If an analytical column has dimensions of 5-25 cm in length and 2-4.6 mm in diameter made of a stainless steel tube, what is the core basis of separation inside it?
questions.diagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 500 160' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='500' height='160' fill='#f8fafc' rx='8'/><text x='250' y='25' font-size='13' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1e293b' font-family='sans-serif'>Stainless Steel Column (5-25 cm) - Partition Principle</text><rect x='80' y='55' width='340' height='70' rx='8' fill='#e2e8f0' stroke='#475569' stroke-width='2'/><text x='250' y='85' font-size='12' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1e293b' font-family='sans-serif'>Stationary Phase Beads (Packed Bed)</text><text x='250' y='105' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle' fill='#0284c7' font-family='sans-serif'>Mobile Phase & Solute Partitioning (K_D)</text></svg>

options.B: Partition/distribution coefficient of the solute between the stationary phase and mobile phase.
options.C: Glass capacity of 1.2 L in solvent reservoirs.

questions.explanation: The core principle of HPLC is partition chromatography, where the solute distributes between the stationary phase (packed particles inside the column) and the mobile phase[span_3](start_span)[span_3](end_span).

questions.question: HPLC detectors are divided into two main categories: Bulk property detectors and Solute property detectors. Under which category does the Refractive Index (RI) detector fall, and what is its limitation?
questions.diagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 500 160' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='500' height='160' fill='#f8fafc' rx='8'/><text x='250' y='25' font-size='13' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1e293b' font-family='sans-serif'>Bulk Property vs Solute Property Detector</text><rect x='50' y='50' width='180' height='75' rx='6' fill='#fce7f3' stroke='#db2777' stroke-width='2'/><text x='140' y='80' font-size='11' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#9d174d' font-family='sans-serif'>Bulk Property (RI / Cond)</text><text x='140' y='105' font-size='9' text-anchor='middle' fill='#831843' font-family='sans-serif'>Sensitive to Gradient Elution</text><rect x='270' y='50' width='180' height='75' rx='6' fill='#ccfbf1' stroke='#0d9488' stroke-width='2'/><text x='360' y='80' font-size='11' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#115e59' font-family='sans-serif'>Solute Property (UV/Vis)</text><text x='360' y='105' font-size='9' text-anchor='middle' fill='#134e4a' font-family='sans-serif'>Independent of Mobile Phase</text></svg>

options.A: Solute property detector; it can be easily used with gradient elution.
options.B: Bulk property detector; it measures differences in physical properties between mobile phase and solute, and is sensitive/unstable for gradient elution.
options.C: Mass spectrometer; it only works after the flow splitting valve.
options.D: Electrochemical detector; it is strictly for UV-active compounds.

questions.explanation: The RI detector is a bulk property detector measuring the bulk property of the mobile phase. Since mobile phase composition changes during gradient elution, the RI detector is unstable with gradients[span_4](start_span)[span_4](end_span).

questions.question: Organic solvents like methanol, Isopropanol (IPA), and water are used in solvent reservoirs. Why are they sonicated or sparged with helium before use?
questions.diagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 500 160' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='500' height='160' fill='#f8fafc' rx='8'/><text x='250' y='25' font-size='13' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1e293b' font-family='sans-serif'>Degassing: Sonication & Helium Sparging</text><rect x='80' y='50' width='120' height='70' rx='6' fill='#dcfce7' stroke='#16a34a' stroke-width='2'/><text x='140' y='80' font-size='11' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#166534' font-family='sans-serif'>Solvent Flask</text><text x='140' y='102' font-size='9' text-anchor='middle' fill='#15803d' font-family='sans-serif'>Methanol / H2O</text><path d='M 230 85 L 270 85 M 250 70 L 250 100' stroke='#ca8a04' stroke-width='3'/><text x='250' y='135' font-size='10' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#854d0e' font-family='sans-serif'>Removes Dissolved Air/Gas</text><rect x='300' y='50' width='120' height='70' rx='6' fill='#e0e7ff' stroke='#4f46e5' stroke-width='2'/><text x='360' y='80' font-size='11' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#3730a3' font-family='sans-serif'>Degasser Unit</text><text x='360' y='102' font-size='9' text-anchor='middle' fill='#4338ca' font-family='sans-serif'>Bubble-Free Flow</text></svg>

options.A: To increase the temperature of the solvents.
options.B: To remove dissolved air and gases to prevent bubble formation.
options.C: To supply 6000 psi pressure to the solvents.
options.D: To make the sample injector automatic.

questions.explanation: Sonication and helium sparging perform degasification, removing trapped or dissolved gases from inside the solvents[span_5](start_span)[span_5](end_span).

questions.question: What function does the loop injector system perform as a sample injector in HPLC?
questions.diagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 500 160' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='500' height='160' fill='#f8fafc' rx='8'/><text x='250' y='25' font-size='13' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1e293b' font-family='sans-serif'>Sample Loop Injector Mechanism</text><line x1='60' y1='85' x2='180' y2='85' stroke='#0284c7' stroke-width='3'/><circle cx='230' cy='85' r='25' fill='#fef08a' stroke='#ca8a04' stroke-width='2'/><text x='230' y='89' font-size='11' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#854d0e' font-family='sans-serif'>Loop</text><line x1='280' y1='85' x2='420' y2='85' stroke='#0284c7' stroke-width='3'/><text x='250' y='130' font-size='10' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#0369a1' font-family='sans-serif'>Introduces Precise Sample Volume into Flowing MP</text></svg>

options.A: It introduces a precise sample volume into the flowing mobile phase.
options.B: It protects the column from high pressure.
options.C: It records UV and IR spectra.
options.D: It sends waste to the recorder.

questions.explanation: The primary use of the loop injector system is to inject the sample into the flowing mobile phase in a reproducible manner[span_6](start_span)[span_6](end_span).

questions.question: If a solute property detector (such as a UV-Vis detector) is being used, what is its characteristic feature regarding the mobile phase?
questions.diagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 500 160' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='500' height='160' fill='#f8fafc' rx='8'/><text x='250' y='25' font-size='13' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1e293b' font-family='sans-serif'>Solute Property Detector (UV-Vis / PDA)</text><rect x='150' y='60' width='200' height='60' rx='6' fill='#bae6fd' stroke='#0284c7' stroke-width='2'/><text x='250' y='95' font-size='12' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#0369a1' font-family='sans-serif'>Ideally Independent of Mobile Phase</text></svg>

options.A: It depends on the bulk property of the mobile phase.
options.B: It is ideally independent of mobile phase properties and responds only to specific physical/chemical characteristics of the solute.
options.D: It reduces the column length to 2 cm.

questions.explanation: Solute property detectors (such as UV, Fluorescence, Electrochemical) detect target analyte properties and are ideally independent of mobile phase background properties[span_7](start_span)[span_7](end_span).

questions.question: What is the use of the flow splitting valve when running HPLC with advanced detectors like Mass Spectrometry (MS)?
questions.diagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 500 160' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='500' height='160' fill='#f8fafc' rx='8'/><text x='250' y='25' font-size='13' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1e293b' font-family='sans-serif'>Flow Splitting Valve (Hyphenated Systems)</text><line x1='60' y1='80' x2='200' y2='80' stroke='#0284c7' stroke-width='3'/><circle cx='220' cy='80' r='12' fill='#fbcfe8' stroke='#db2777' stroke-width='2'/><text x='220' y='84' font-size='9' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#be185d' font-family='sans-serif'>Split</text><line x1='232' y1='80' x2='380' y2='50' stroke='#0284c7' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='232' y1='80' x2='380' y2='110' stroke='#0284c7' stroke-width='2'/><text x='420' y='55' font-size='10' font-weight='bold' fill='#0369a1'>Main Detector</text><text x='420' y='115' font-size='10' font-weight='bold' fill='#be185d'>Sensitive MS Fraction</text></svg>

options.A: It checks the methanol level in the solvent reservoirs.
options.B: It divides the total flow rate so that only a small fraction goes to a sensitive detector (like MS).
options.C: It maintains the pump pressure above 6000 psi.

questions.explanation: The flow splitting valve splits the mobile phase flow, which is necessary for certain detectors (like MS or hyphenated systems) where high flow rates can overload the detector[span_8](start_span)[span_8](end_span).

questions.question: If the normal flow rate in an HPLC system is 1.2 ml/min and the pump can generate a maximum pressure of 6000 psi, what will happen to the system if a blockage occurs in the column?
questions.diagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 500 160' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='500' height='160' fill='#f8fafc' rx='8'/><text x='250' y='25' font-size='13' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1e293b' font-family='sans-serif'>Column Blockage & Pressure Spike (upto 6000 psi)</text><rect x='100' y='60' width='300' height='50' rx='6' fill='#fee2e2' stroke='#dc2626' stroke-width='2'/><text x='250' y='91' font-size='12' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#991b1b' font-family='sans-serif'>Blockage Detected -> Pressure Drastically Increases</text></svg>

options.A: The pump pressure will increase drastically.
options.B: The flow rate will automatically double.
options.C: The glass capacity of solvent reservoirs will become 2 L.
options.D: The detector will automatically turn off.

questions.explanation: When a blockage occurs in the column or frits, fluid resistance increases, forcing the pump to increase pressure significantly to maintain the same flow rate[span_9](start_span)[span_9](end_span).

questions.question: What is the typical capacity of glass solvent reservoirs and why is glass used as their material?
questions.diagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 500 160' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='500' height='160' fill='#f8fafc' rx='8'/><text x='250' y='25' font-size='13' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1e293b' font-family='sans-serif'>Glass Solvent Reservoir (1 - 2 Liter Capacity)</text><rect x='180' y='45' width='140' height='90' rx='10' fill='#f1f5f9' stroke='#334155' stroke-width='2'/><text x='250' y='90' font-size='12' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#334155' font-family='sans-serif'>Inert Glass</text><text x='250' y='110' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle' fill='#16a34a' font-family='sans-serif'>Capacity: 1 - 2 Liters</text></svg>

options.A: 1-2 L capacity; for chemical inertness and transparency so the solvent level is visible.
options.B: 10-25 cm capacity; to be strong like stainless steel.
options.C: 6000 psi capacity; to withstand high pressure.
options.D: 1.2 ml capacity; to match the flow rate.

questions.explanation: Solvent reservoirs are typically made of 1-2 L glass so they remain inert to organic solvents and the internal volume is easily visible[span_10](start_span)[span_10](end_span).

questions.question: If you need to check the purity of a pharmaceutical compound that is not UV active but shows a refractive index, which detector would you choose and why?
questions.diagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 500 160' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='500' height='160' fill='#f8fafc' rx='8'/><text x='250' y='25' font-size='13' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1e293b' font-family='sans-serif'>Non-UV Active Compound Analysis</text><rect x='100' y='60' width='300' height='50' rx='6' fill='#e0f2fe' stroke='#0284c7' stroke-width='2'/><text x='250' y='91' font-size='12' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#0369a1' font-family='sans-serif'>Use Refractive Index (RI) Bulk Detector</text></svg>

options.A: UV-Vis detector, because it is a solute property detector.
options.B: Refractive Index (RI) detector, because it is a bulk property detector that can detect non-UV active solutes.
options.C: Fluorescence detector, because it is independent of the mobile phase.
options.D: Electrochemical detector with flow splitting valve.

questions.explanation: For non-UV active compounds (like sugars or polymers), UV detectors do not work, so bulk property detectors like the Refractive Index (RI) detector are used[span_11](start_span)[span_11](end_span).

questions.question: According to the instrumentation diagram, after the sample injector, where do the mobile phase and sample travel before entering the analytical column?
questions.diagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 500 160' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='500' height='160' fill='#f8fafc' rx='8'/><text x='250' y='25' font-size='13' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1e293b' font-family='sans-serif'>Flow Path: Injector -> Guard -> Analytical Column</text><line x1='50' y1='85' x2='150' y2='85' stroke='#0284c7' stroke-width='3'/><rect x='150' y='65' width='80' height='40' rx='4' fill='#86efac' stroke='#166534' stroke-width='2'/><text x='190' y='90' font-size='10' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#14532d' font-family='sans-serif'>Guard Col</text><line x1='230' y1='85' x2='290' y2='85' stroke='#0284c7' stroke-width='3'/><rect x='290' y='55' width='150' height='60' rx='6' fill='#fca5a5' stroke='#991b1b' stroke-width='2'/><text x='365' y='90' font-size='11' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#7f1d1d' font-family='sans-serif'>Analytical Column</text></svg>
questions.explanation: After sample injection, the flow passes through the pre-column (guard column), which protects the main analytical column from impurities[span_12](start_span)[span_12](end_span).

questions.question: If gradient elution needs to be used instead of isocratic elution in an HPLC system, what combination of mixing valve and pump works?
questions.diagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 500 160' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='500' height='160' fill='#f8fafc' rx='8'/><text x='250' y='25' font-size='13' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1e293b' font-family='sans-serif'>Gradient Elution: Variable Solvent Mixing Ratio</text><rect x='100' y='60' width='300' height='50' rx='6' fill='#e0e7ff' stroke='#4f46e5' stroke-width='2'/><text x='250' y='91' font-size='12' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle' fill='#3730a3' font-family='sans-serif'>Dynamic Composition Change over Time</text></svg>

options.A: The proportion of solvents from multiple reservoirs is dynamically changed during the run.
options.B: Only a single solvent reservoir can be used.
options.C: The column length is mechanically lengthened.
options.D: The flow rate is set to zero.

questions.question: In the final stage of HPLC instrumentation, where are components routed after the detector?
